newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: El Nino to be top topic at world weather meet.
newsitem.headline: El Nino to be top topic at world weather meet.

text.p: About 1,500 scientists from around the world will meet in the Australian city of Melbourne next week for nine days of information-sharing on one of the hottest topics of the time -- weather.
The conference, informally titled "Earth, Ocean, Atmosphere: Forces for Change" and one of the largest scientific meetings ever in the southern hemisphere, could hardly be better timed.
Australia this year faces a strengthening El Nino weather effect which threatens to devastate crops with drought.
El Nino, the product of interaction of warm Pacific Ocean temperatures off the South American coast with atmospheric conditions, is not just an Australian concern.

It also threatens dry weather in Southeast Asia, particularly Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea. And typically, when it produces bushfires and drought in eastern Australia, El Nino also brings rains and floods in California.
El Nino and its opposite, La Nina (Australia wet/California dry), will be one of the major themes of the Melbourne conference, which begins on Tuesday and continues until July 9.
The other major theme, presented by Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) and the Bureau of Meteorology, will be greenhouse global warming.
The conference will also cover the entire range of weather effects, from tsunamis (tidal waves) to earthquakes, to drought and floods and to glaciers.

One paper showed that El Nino was not nearly as powerful a force in Australia 6,000 years ago as today, Paul Holper, communications manager for the CSIRO's atmospheric research division, told Reuters on Wednesday.
This conclusion is based on an examination of coral records on the Great Barrier Reef.

Other papers revealed the latest on extreme events, he said. One showed that an 80 metre (260 feet) high tsunami hit Australia's New South Wales coast in the past 1,000 years, depositing debris 20-30 kilometres (12-20 miles) inland.
Another paper showed that glaciers affected Australia's island state of Tasmania in the past 10,000 years, he said.
Papers on greenhouse global warming would show latest effects on ice caps and warming in Antarctica.
The conference is not designed to come to major conclusions or present breakthrough evidence, Holper said.
"Its more of a big information-sharing session than (aimed at) coming up with major policy suggestions," he said.
Abstracts of other papers show:
-- Ocean warming has been detected near Antarctica.
-- Atlantic sea surface temperature anomalies, weaker than those of the Pacific, can still cause disastrous climate hazards over the Americas and Africa.

-- Drought in northeast Brazil is closley related to tropical Atlantic sea surface temperature variability, while rainfall variability in the Sahel region of Africa has been linked with temperature fluctuations in the tropical Atlantic.
-- Warm waters south of the equator in the western Pacific may cause more powerful east Asian monsoons than normal.

"Climate is one of the most naturally disastrous and disruptive forces affecting human society and the strongest cause of climate fluctuations is the El Nino," R.H. Kripalani and Ashwini Kulkarni of the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, India, say in a paper.
"The majority of droughts over the Asian region are related to the El Nino."
